executive_summary: The Active Directory domain DOMAIN-1 exhibits an extremely critical security posture with a hygiene score of 1 out of 100, indicating widespread misconfigurations and multiple pathways to complete domain compromise. Intruders can leverage unpatched vulnerabilities like ZeroLogon and noPac alongside severe certificate services misconfigurations (such as ESC1, ESC15, and ESC8 NTLM relay) to rapidly escalate privileges to Tier 0. Furthermore, critical infrastructure weaknesses include writable SYSVOL shares, exposed Group Policy Preferences passwords, and multiple accounts with unrotated credentials or dangerous delegated permissions. Immediate intervention is required to patch domain controllers, harden AD CS templates, secure SYSVOL permissions, and revoke unauthorized administrative and replication rights.

remediation_plan.title: Harden Active Directory Certificate Services (AD CS) and Disable Vulnerable Templates
remediation_plan.rationale: Removes multiple critical escalation paths (ESC1, ESC2, ESC3, ESC4, ESC8, ESC13, ESC15) that allow low-privileged users to request high-privilege or client-authentication certificates for immediate domain takeover.
remediation_plan.caveats: Disabling or modifying certificate templates and CA settings may impact applications requiring automated enrollment. Test template modifications in a staging environment before production deployment.

remediation_plan.title: Patch Domain Controllers and Enforce Secure Channels
remediation_plan.rationale: Closes critical execution and impersonation vectors (ZeroLogon, noPac) and prevents NTLM relay attacks against domain controllers by enforcing signing and channel binding.
remediation_plan.caveats: Enforcing LDAP signing and channel binding can break legacy applications relying on unsigned or unchannel-bound LDAP queries. Audit legacy traffic prior to enforcement.

remediation_plan.title: Secure SYSVOL, GPOs, and Remove Hardcoded Credentials
remediation_plan.rationale: Stops attackers from modifying Group Policy Objects or planting scripts and credentials in SYSVOL to achieve arbitrary code execution on domain controllers and workstations.
remediation_plan.caveats: Ensure deployment scripts or administrative tools do not rely on writable SYSVOL paths or embedded credentials before revoking permissions.

remediation_plan.title: Revoke Unauthorized Tier 0 Permissions and Clean Up Dangerous ACLs
remediation_plan.rationale: Eliminates excessive administrative privileges and dangerous access controls (such as unauthorized DCSync rights, AdminSDHolder modifications, and readable gMSA/LAPS secrets) granted to non-Tier 0 principals.
remediation_plan.caveats: Removing permissions from built-in or integration accounts (such as Exchange Windows Permissions or sync accounts) requires validating proper split-permissions configurations and administrative boundaries.

remediation_plan.title: Rotate and Secure Privileged Credentials and Kerberos Settings
remediation_plan.rationale: Mitigates Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, and ticket forgery attacks by enforcing strong encryption types (AES), disabling pre-authentication requirements, and rotating long-lived credentials.
remediation_plan.caveats: Rotating the krbtgt password twice in succession invalidates all existing Kerberos tickets. Ensure domain replication is healthy before rotation.

remediation_plan.title: Harden Domain Controller Services and Attack Surface Configurations
remediation_plan.rationale: Disables unnecessary services (Print Spooler, WebClient) and insecure authentication features (WDigest, basic WinRM) on domain controllers to prevent coercion and local credential harvesting.
remediation_plan.caveats: Verify whether printing services or legacy web-based management tools depend on the Print Spooler or WebClient before disabling.

quick_wins: Disable the WebClient service via GPO across all domain controllers to mitigate web-based NTLM coercion vectors.
Disable WDigest authentication via GPO on domain controllers to prevent cleartext credential caching in LSASS.
Enforce strong Kerberos encryption types and disable RC4/DES where possible across domain controllers.
Remove unnecessary accounts from privileged groups such as Domain Admins and Backup Operators.
Enable Account Lockout threshold settings in the Default Domain Policy to prevent brute-force attacks.

monitoring.guidance: Monitor for Directory Service Access events (4662) where the DS-Replication-Get-Changes or DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All extended rights are requested against the domain object by non-standard accounts.

Monitor AD CS Certificate Services audit logs for event IDs 4886 (certificate request received) and 4887 (certificate issued), paying attention to requests containing alternative subject names or unusual user principal names.
Monitor System and Security logs for Netlogon secure channel establishment attempts using vulnerable cryptographic algorithms or anomalous computer account creation bursts (Event 4741).

Detect potential Kerberoasting activity by monitoring for Kerberos service ticket requests (Event 4769) requesting RC4 encryption (0x17) or high volumes of TGS requests from a single user account in a short timeframe.

Monitor for anomalous network logon events (Event 4624 with Logon Type 3) using NTLM authentication against domain controllers, especially originating from unexpected internal hosts or service accounts.

attack_paths.title: Kerberoasting Privileged Accounts
steps: USER-14 -> Request service ticket for SPN backup/HOSTFQDN-34
attack_paths.narrative: An attacker with standard domain user access requests a Kerberos service ticket for a privileged service account with a weak password, cracks it offline, and gains administrative control.

attack_paths.title: AD CS ESC1 Certificate Enrollment
steps: NETBIOS-1\Domain Users -> Enroll in TEMPLATE-1 with alternate subject name
TEMPLATE-1 -> Authenticate as Domain Admin using issued certificate
attack_paths.narrative: Low-privileged domain users can request certificates from a vulnerable template supplying an arbitrary subject name mapped to a privileged account, achieving full domain compromise.

attack_paths.title: RBCD Delegation Abuse against Domain Controllers
steps: HOST-7$ -> Configure Resource-Based Constrained Delegation on DC-1$
DC-1$ -> Impersonate privileged user via S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy
attack_paths.narrative: Control over an object with RBCD configured targeting a domain controller allows an intruder to forge authentication tickets for privileged users, leading to Tier 0 control.

attack_paths.title: DCSync via Direct Domain Rights
steps: NETBIOS-1\USER-31 -> Invoke DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All on domain head
attack_paths.narrative: An account holding explicit DCSync replication rights can replicate all domain password hashes directly from the domain controllers, achieving full domain compromise.

attack_paths.title: GPO Abuse Leading to DC Control
steps: GPO-1 -> Modify machine startup script or tasks linked to Domain Controllers OU
GPO-1 -> Execute arbitrary code on domain controllers
attack_paths.narrative: Control over a GPO linked to the Domain Controllers OU allows an intruder to deploy malicious startup scripts or tasks executed with SYSTEM privileges on all domain controllers.

attack_paths.title: Unconstrained Delegation Exploitation
steps: HOST-2$ -> Wait for privileged user authentication or coerce connection
HOST-2$ -> Capture TGT from memory cache
attack_paths.narrative: Compromise of a non-DC computer configured with unconstrained delegation allows capture of forwarded Kerberos TGTs from administrative users connecting to the host.

remediation_scripts.caveats: Clearing EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 removes requester-supplied SAN support on the CA. Verify that no legitimate applications rely on this flag before executing.
Disables WDigest cleartext credential caching in LSASS. Requires a reboot or service restart to take full effect.
Stops and disables the WebClient service to prevent WebDAV-based NTLM coercion.

triage.rationale: Direct DCSync rights grant immediate ability to extract all domain password hashes and achieve full domain compromise.
Allows low-privileged users to request certificates for arbitrary accounts including Domain Admins.
Unpatched domain controller vulnerabilities allow unauthenticated attackers to elevate to Domain Admin instantly.
Writable SYSVOL and exposed GPP passwords enable trivial code execution and credential theft across the domain.
Exposes privileged service and user accounts to offline brute-force credential recovery.

known_exploitation.public: Widely exploited by ransomware groups and threat actors for initial domain takeover via Netlogon cryptographic weakness.
known_exploitation.relevance: Domain controllers have weakened Netlogon secure channel enforcement, permitting immediate exploitation.

known_exploitation.public: Extensively used in intrusion campaigns to spoof domain controller computer accounts and escalate privileges.
known_exploitation.relevance: Domain controller DCHOST-2 lacks the necessary security updates and permits high machine account quotas.

known_exploitation.vector: AD CS Certificate Template Abuse & NTLM Relay (ESC1 / ESC8)
known_exploitation.public: Core vector in numerous ransomware and APT intrusions involving Active Directory Certificate Services exploitation.
known_exploitation.relevance: Templates allow requester-supplied subject names and web enrollment is active without adequate protection.

known_exploitation.public: Standard automated check in nearly all penetration tests and red team engagements targeting Windows domains.
known_exploitation.relevance: Exposed cpassword strings found in SYSVOL files.

known_exploitation.public: Pervasive technique in enterprise intrusions through 2026 for extracting service account credentials.
known_exploitation.relevance: Multiple privileged and standard user accounts feature Service Principal Names with old or weak passwords.

compromise_assessment.summary: An attacker with standard domain user access can leverage multiple independent paths to achieve full domain compromise, including certificate template abuse (ESC1), Kerberoasting of privileged accounts, and exploiting unpatched domain controller vulnerabilities.

chains.title: AD CS ESC1 Certificate Escalation

links.gives: Ability to request a certificate as a Domain Admin

break_point.why: Disabling or reconfiguring TEMPLATE-1 removes enrollee-supplied subject capability.

chains.narrative: A standard domain user requests a certificate via TEMPLATE-1 specifying a Domain Admin principal in the subject alternative name, authenticates via Schannel, and gains Tier 0 control.

chains.title: Privileged Kerberoasting

links.gives: Kerberos service ticket for a Domain Admin account
links.assumption: Password is weak enough to crack offline

break_point.why: Removing SPNs from privileged accounts or enforcing strong, frequently rotated passwords stops offline cracking.

chains.narrative: An attacker requests a service ticket for USER-6 (Domain Admin), cracks the ticket offline, and uses the recovered password to authenticate as a Domain Admin.

chains.title: DCSync via Explicit Rights

break_point.why: Removing the explicit DCSync ACE from NETBIOS-1\USER-31 prevents unauthorized replication.

chains.narrative: Compromising USER-31 allows the principal to invoke directory replication functions against the domain root and extract all domain secrets.

chains.title: GPO Abuse leading to Domain Controller Code Execution

links.gives: GenericWrite over GPO-1 linked to Domain Controllers OU
Execution of arbitrary code on domain controllers
links.assumption: Attacker can write to PATH-4 share

break_point.why: Revoking GenericWrite permissions on GPO-1 stops unauthorized GPO modification.

chains.narrative: Members of GROUP-5 modify GPO-1 to execute scripts or tasks on domain controllers during startup, yielding complete control over all DCs.

rejected_chains.title: Anonymous LDAP Enumeration to Domain Compromise
rejected_chains.reason: While anonymous LDAP operations are enabled via dSHeuristics, anonymous access alone does not grant write or administrative privileges required for domain control without an additional credential or exploit chain.

verify_next.question: Are vulnerable AD CS certificate templates (such as TEMPLATE-1 and TEMPLATE-13) actively monitored or restricted by application controls?
Is network reachability restricted between workstations and domain controllers for WebDAV/RPC coercion vectors?
Are the accounts flagged for Kerberoasting (USER-6, USER-14) protected by exceptionally long, randomly generated passwords?
Is network traffic between domain controllers and member servers subjected to mandatory SMB and LDAP signing in practice?
